Abdul Quayum with Mokbul Hossain and Swapan Kumar Dutta, Advocates — For the Petitioners. 
Syed Mokaddas Ali with Rowshan Ara Begum, Advocates — For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Shamsul Hoque and others ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Moze Ali Mollah and ors ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the defendant Nos. 9 and 15 arising out of an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure calls in question the judgment and decree dated 20-1-1993 passed by the Sub-ordinate Judge, Patuakhali in Title Appeal No. 83 of 1989 reversing the judgment and decree dated 26-7-1989 passed by the Assistant Judge, Bauphal Upazila in Title Suit No. 7 of 1987 dismissing the suit.

2. Fact relevant for the disposal of the present Rule is that, the plaintiff-opposite parties filed the aforesaid title suit for a declaration that the order of mutation passed in Mutation Case No. 193(11) Bau-68-69 and order dated 18-11-86 passed in Miscellaneous Case No.32 BPL/83-84 are illegal and not binding on them alleging, inter alia, that they are the heirs of the SA recorded tenants and are all along in possession of the suit land. The plaintiff opposite parties for the first time came to learn in 1984 from the local Tahsildar that the suit lands were mutated in the names of the defendant-petitioners. Accordingly, plaintiff-opposite parties made an enquiry into the matter and came to know that the defendant-petitioners managed to mutate their names in respect of the suit land in the aforesaid Mutation Case No. 193(11) Bau-68-69 on the basis of some false and manufactured documents showing that the defendant-petitioners auction-purchased the suit land pursuant to Mortgage Execution Case No. 32 of 1951 on the basis of a mortgage decree in Title Suit No. 102 of 1949 and that the mutation was done without serving any notice on them. Accordingly, the plaintiff-opposite parties filed Miscellaneous Case No. 32 BPL/83-84 before the Revenue Authority concerned for reconsideration of the aforesaid mutation order. But the Revenue Authority refused to reconsider its earlier order passed in favour of the defendant-petitioners in 1969. The plaintiff-opposite parties asserted that the aforesaid mortgage suit, mortgage decree and auction-purchase of the suit land and delivery of possession thereof in favour of the defendant-petitioners were all false and manufactured and the defendant-petitioners did not have any possession of the suit land at any time.

3. The petitioners as defendant Nos. 9 and 15 only contested the suit by filing written statement, contending, inter alia, that they auction purchased the suit land in auction in Mortgage Execution Case No. 32 of 1951 arising out of a mortgage decree passed in Title Suit No. 102 of 1949 and accordingly, they obtained mutation order in their names as far back as in 1969 under section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act by the relevant revenue authority and as such the suit was liable to be dismissed.

4. The plaintiff-opposite parties examined 4 PWs and the defendant-petitioners, on the other hand, examined 2 DWs in support of their respective case. During the trial the plaintiff-opposite parties proved and exhibited SA and RS Khatians and the defendant-petitioner filed and proved relevant documents showing that there was a mortgage suit and the suit land was subsequently purchased in auction-sale by them in execution of a mortgage decree by filing an execution case and got possession thereof.

5. The trial Court, however, dismissed the suit on the finding that the plaintiff-opposite parties ought to have challenged the auction-purchase by the defendant-petitioners pursuant to the mortgage decree and not the order of mutation made in the year 1969 and that the plaintiff-opposite parties had no possession of the suit land.

6. On an appeal by the plaintiff-opposite parties the appellate Court below decreed the suit by reversing the judgment and decree of the trial Court only on point of law namely, that the order of mutation passed by the revenue authority in 1969 under section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in favour of the defendant-petitioners setting aside the entries in the SA Khatian was without jurisdiction and was thus liable to be set aside.

7. Mr Abdul Quayum, learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioners, submits that since the instant suit is not maintainable being hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, the trial Court rightly dismissed the same and the appellate Court below committed an error of law by decreeing the same when it was liable to be dismissed in limini. The learned Advocate elaborating his augment submits that the plaintiff-opposite parties had no locus standi to file the present suit inasmuch as they could not be said to have any legal character or right to property in respect of the suit land inasmuch as SA Khatian standing in their names had no presumptive value as regards proprietary right to the suit land. It is also contended by the learned Advocate that the suit is not maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act as the plaintiff-opposite parties failed to seek any declaration as to their own status and also failed to pray for a further or consequential relief by way of possession. In support of his aforesaid submissions the learned Advocate referred to and relied on the cases reported in 18 DLR 706, to show that the plaintiff must have legal character or right to property, 6 BCR (AD) 57 showing that mere declaration in the absence of consequential relief is fatal, 42 DLR 24 and 13 DLR 676 showing that symbolical possession by defendant requires plaintiff to seek relief for recovery of possession. The learned Advocate also relied on the case reported in 19 DLR 9 in support of his contention that the SA Khatian does not give rise to any presumption of title to the suit land.

8. Mr Syed Mokaddas Ali, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite parties, submits opposing the Rule that since the impugned order of mutation passed by the revenue authority in 1969 purportedly under section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was without jurisdiction the appellate court below rightly decreed the suit by reversing the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court. The learned Advocate also submits that the plaintiff-opposite parties being the heirs of SA recorded tenants in respect of the suit land had locus standi to file the suit for declaration to the above effect and in view of the nature of declaration sought for there was no necessity to pay for any further or consequential relief.

<u>9. Admittedly, both the SA Khatians as well as RS Khatians in respect of the suit land stand in the names of the predecessors-in-interest of the plaintiff-opposite parties and also in some of their names. It is true that the SA records, in view of section 19(3) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, do not provide conclusive evidence as regards title but it provides conclusive evidence as regards their preparation and revision. But entries in the SA records; in my opinion, provide a prima facie evidence as regards title. In order to maintain a suit for declaration under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, the plaintiff is required to have prima facie evidence showing that he has a legal character or right to a property in respect of the subject matter of the suit and granting or refusal to grant a decree in such suit shall always depend on final adjudication thereof on evidence. Since the SA records vide Exts 3 and 3(Ka) stand in the names of the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiff-opposite parties and also in some of their names it should be taken to be a prima facie evidence of title of the plaintiff-opposite parties in respect of the suit land and, as such, the plaintiff-opposite parties were competent to file the present suit. I do not dispute the legal principles deduced in the aforesaid cases cited by the learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioners. Since the present suit was not for a declaration of title but for a declaration of the act of the revenue authority namely, the order of mutation outside the purview of law as illegal the same is certainly maintainable. Reference may be made in this connection to the case reported in 16 DLR 298.</u>

10. Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act is not exhaustive but it does not sanction every form of declaration but only a declaration that the plaintiff is entitled to a specific legal character or right as to the property. In other words, a suit under this section cannot be maintained unless the plaintiff is a person entitled to some legal character or to such right as to property.

<u>11. In terms of the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act the court shall in exercise of its discretion refuse to grant any declaration if the plaintiff being in a position to seek further relief than a mere declaration of title fails to do so. Because the object of the proviso is to avoid multiplicity of suits and to prevent a person from getting a mere declaration of his rights in one suit and to resort to any remedy which was already available to him. A consequential relief is one which directly flows from the decree passed. A consequential relief within the meaning of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, however, must fulfil another condition namely, the relief must be asked for as an incidental to the declaratory decree. In the present case the plaintiff-opposite parties being SA recorded tenant merely sought for a declaration that the mutation order which was passed in 1969 affecting their proprietary right in respect of the suit lands was bad in law. If a decree is passed to the above effect the purpose of the plaintiff-opposite parties would be served and they are not required, in my view, to ask for any consequential or further relief by way of recovery of possession. Because such further relief is not at all necessary in view of the declaratory relief granted in this case.</u>

<u>12. A suit for declaration simpliciter in a case, such as the present one, is maintainable without any further or consequential relief by way of recovery of khas possession, since the mutation order was challenged as made in excess of jurisdiction in the interest of maintenance or preservation of legal and proper act namely, the preparation of SA record.</u>

13. The Revenue Authority in this case is palpably without jurisdiction in disturbing the entries in the SA record in the name of mutation at the instance of the defendant-petitioners in purported exercise of powers under section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

<u>14. Section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is attracted only when clerical mistake is required to be corrected or a mutation of names is to be made as a result of transfer or inheritance. It is not attracted when the record of right is to be corrected after a finding to be given as to the title of holders or challengers. The examination of title deeds for the purpose of determining title to the holder of record of rights is not permissible under section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The word ''transfer'' in Clause (a) of section 143 of the said Act is limited to transfer by the recorded tenants and not by other persons. In the present case the mutation was sought for by the defendant-petitioners not because of the transfer by the plaintiff-opposite parties, but on account of auction sale at the instance of the court due to a mortgage decree. In that view of the matter, the impugned mutation order in favour of the defendant-petitioners by the revenue authority was without jurisdiction. Moreover, all the four PWs as well as DWs 1 and 2 have stated in their evidence that the plaintiff-opposite parties are in possession of the suit land. The appellate Court below has, therefore, rightly decreed that suit in favour of the plaintiff-opposite parties.</u>

In the result, the Rule is discharged and the judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court below decreeing the suit is hereby confirmed without any order as to costs.

End.
